characterList.description: An older man with short white hair, wearing a light brown jacket over a blue shirt and red tie. He is being interviewed.
characterList.name: John McDonnell

content_metadata.description: Interview with John McDonnell on austerity and political action.

qAndA.answer: The bucket suggests that the protesters are collecting donations or supplies, highlighting the need for support among those affected by austerity measures.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the white bucket seen in the background at 0:37?

qAndA.answer: He draws a parallel between the current economic hardship and the Great Depression of the 1930s, emphasizing the severity of the situation.
qAndA.question: Why does John McDonnell refer to the 1930s when discussing poverty?

qAndA.answer: He wants the TUC (Trades Union Congress) to coordinate industrial action, implying a need for a united front against the government's policies.
qAndA.question: What specific action does John McDonnell call for regarding the TUC?

qAndA.answer: The Occupy movement is a global protest movement against economic inequality. John McDonnell sees it as a way for people to get involved in discussing and challenging the current political and economic system.
qAndA.question: What is the Occupy movement, and why does John McDonnell mention it?

qAndA.answer: He believes that a Labour government is necessary for a significant redistribution of power and wealth, aiming to alleviate the suffering of millions of people.
qAndA.question: What is John McDonnell's ultimate goal in advocating for a Labour government?

activities.description: John McDonnell is being interviewed and he is speaking to the camera.

characterInteraction.description: John McDonnell interacts with the interviewer offscreen, answering their questions about poverty, strikes, and the upcoming election.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The interview highlights a deep distrust in the government and a sense of powerlessness among working-class people. The call to action emphasizes the importance of collective action and solidarity in fighting against injustice.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: We're standing in Parliament Square at the moment, opposite the House of Commons.
And the reason that we're here is because this weekend, during the demonstrations that
were taken place and the strikes were taken place, people wanted to also demonstrate solidarity.
The way that they're doing that is they're occupying Parliament Square.
This has always been a public square for the use of people to debate and raise issues.
They're using it to have a debate about what to absolutely really be, to how we can be
properly represented.
So in Parliament Square at the moment, despite all the police intimidation, people are coming
here and having a proper debate about the use of the debate.
As you mentioned police intimidation, we just get a shot of those people who have been
out on strike in the last week.
We had midwives and other workers in the NHS last Monday, jobs centre staff on Wednesday,
and then today this Monday we've had the Society of Radiographers out on strike.
What's your position on those strikes?
I have support of 100% having on the picket lines, the health picket lines and civil service
picket lines.
It's interesting, isn't it?
We've got people coming out on strike now, there's unions have never been on strike for
a century or at all, and it's because of the depth of anger that people feel.
You can feel people suffering in my community at the moment.
We're experiencing a wave of poverty that we've not seen maybe since the 1930s, the housing
situation's a nightmare.
People are probably difficult to put food on the tables, and million families now a year
go to food banks.
In addition to that, we're having people sanctioned and losing their benefits altogether.
So absolute poverty is now taking place.
So you can see why people in work are coming out on strike.
And remember, 2,000 are the children that are living in poverty in our country.
I didn't found those that are in work, so the wages are just not good enough.
From the five years between September 2009 and sorry from March 2009 to March 2014, the
wages are fallen by, for the average person, £1,750 a year.
So why do you think that's happened, first of all, and what can we do about it?
That's a deliberate policy of the coalition government, who effectively, a simply, a simply
representatives of the city of London, the rich and the corporations.
And they're trying to use this crisis, not just to ensure that working class people
just pay for the crisis, but also to shift wealth and power back into their hands.
And there'll be a very successful that.
The richest people in this country and the corporations are having a field day.
They have made billions.
Their last figure I think, chance is the crisis started.
There's something that had increased about 47 billion in the richest, in the hands of the richest people.
So this is all about making working class people pay for the crisis and then ripping them off in the meantime.
That's why people are so angry.
People are angry that they're having to pay for the crisis.
That was caused by not them, but by bankers and others.
But at the same time, the corporations are exploiting the crisis.
Energy prices going up.
Fires are in the shops going up.
Rents increasing.
People are not being able to afford their mortgages, ripped off time and time again.
That's why people are angry and I'm bloody angry about it as well.
What can we do about it?
We can mobilize, first of all.
If you're in a union, if you're not in a union, join a union, if you're in work,
if you're in a union, make sure that union is mobilized.
And the best form mobilization is to take industrial action.
And the best form of industrial action is not when one union comes out on strike,
but when we all come out together, we're called for the team you've seen now
to start coordinating industrial action so it could be effective.
If you're not in work, there are ways in which you can link up with the trade union movement.
For example, the United has this community of memberships, they can join that.
But also, you should be campaigning on individual issues.
Joining some of the social movements that are taking place.
UK Uncup demand that people with organizations pay their taxes,
de-packed disabled people against the cuts, campaigning against cuts
and benefits of people with disabilities.
There's a whole range of social movements now that you can join and get involved in.
The most important thing is to link up.
One of the things you can get involved in now is taking place in Karmie Square
in Central London.
And there's the Occupy group.
Occupy have always been a group of people that come together,
when necessary, to debate the main issues that are affecting our country.
One of the main issues is democracy and how we're not being represented.
So an Occupy is an ideal vehicle for people to get involved in.
Why should people who are working class people in the Labour movement
or people in the anti-Orstereoty movement?
Why should they vote Labour in the upcoming general election?
Well, the most important thing is that they vote.
And they vote for candidates who are standing against austerity.
The Labour Party still has the support of working class people.
And on that basis is the only party that could form a government
which is associated with the working class.
The Labour Party at the moment, its policies are, well, best described by saying
it's austerity life.
So they're saying they'll reverse some of the current government's policies.
But they're still going to implement some of the cuts that are there
in her to the last government.
So the battle actually is, yes, get a Labour government elected,
but the battle is then to make sure that Labour government reflects
what we really need in this country, which is a significant redistribution of power
and wealth.
And in that way, we may be able to change the lives of millions of people
who are suffering under this government.
Thank you.

youtube_description:
Two members of Stroud Against the Cuts presented a workshop at the Occupy Democracy protest camp in Parliament Square in London on Monday 20th October.
As they were about to leave, John McDonnell, Labour MP for Hayes & Harlington in West London, arrived to listen to a workshop being given by Linda Kaucher of Stop TTIP UK.
Before John joined the workshop, we grabbed a quick interview with him on the recent strikes by NHS, civil service and other workers, on falling wages and rising poverty, and on who people should vote for in the General Election in 2015.
youtube_title: John McDonnell, Labour MP for Hayes & Harlington, interviewed by Stroud Against the Cuts
